implementation_notes: Modern C++ ships the pattern in <future>: std::async(std::launch::async, f, args...) starts the call on a new thread of execution and returns std::future<T> immediately; get() is the collect step, blocking until the shared state is ready and rethrowing the exception the callable stored there, while wait_for/wait_until add the timeout variant. A future returned by std::async with launch::async may wait in its destructor; a future from std::promise or std::packaged_task does not join an arbitrary worker thread, so the executor owns thread lifetime. std::packaged_task and std::promise create the same shared state when scheduling is done by hand (a thread pool or a reactor owns the execution), and std::shared_future allows several collectors. The classic callback-object structure is only worth writing when continuations or executor composition are needed, which std::future does not provide - reach for a library (Asio, Folly) or the C++20 coroutine variant instead.
pitfalls: The default policy is launch::async | launch::deferred: the callable may be deferred and then executed inline in whichever thread first waits, so pass std::launch::async explicitly when a real background call is required.
The future returned by std::async blocks in its destructor; discarding the handle turns the asynchronous call back into a synchronous one.
std::future is a unique reference: it is not copyable and get() may be called only once - use std::shared_future for multiple consumers.
An exception stored in a shared state that nobody reads is silently discarded, and a std::future destroyed while a deferred task has not run discards that task.

variants.name: C++20 coroutines: co_await over the async operation
variants.implementation_notes: With C++20 the callback/continuation layer is written by the compiler: a function containing co_await becomes a coroutine whose state is stored separately from the stack, so the asynchronous operation is invoked, the coroutine suspends and the caller's own frame continues - the pattern's start-now step - and resumption on completion supplies the value, which is the collect step expressed as ordinary sequential code. Suspension is stackless and allocation of the coroutine state happens once, so the per-call overhead is smaller than a thread hand-off, but the coroutine must be driven by an executor that resumes it (an Asio io_context, a task scheduler), and the awaited type must model the awaiter/promise protocol. Prefer it where the toolchain is C++20 and the completion-handler pyramid hurts readability; keep std::async/std::future for one-off calls and for code that must compile as C++11.
pitfalls: A coroutine is lazy by construction: nothing executes until the task is awaited or explicitly started, so a discarded task silently performs no work.
The coroutine frame must outlive the awaited operation; dangling references captured in the frame (a reference to a local of a dead caller) are the coroutine-era version of the dangling-callback bug.
Unhandled exceptions inside a coroutine terminate the program unless the promise type or the awaiter converts them into the result channel.
Library composition is non-portable: Asio awaitables, std::execution senders and hand-rolled tasks do not interoperate without adapters - pick one ecosystem per codebase.
